Posted January 22, 2005
Analysis by Richard Cowan Sponsored by Advanced Nutrients

(MarijuanaNews note: On Tuesday, the Vancouver Sun, which has endorsed the legalization of cannabis, ran a bit of prohibitionist propaganda under the headline: B.C. jails one in 7 pot growers Vancouver jails only one in 13 cultivation Lax sentences attract U.S. growers, says drug inspector.

Regular readers of MarijuanaNews will recognize this as a major theme of the Canadian prohibitionist party line. Oh, if we would just punish growers more, there would be less cannabis just like the wonderful USA where everything is just fine. Or something like that.
See
 The Agenda for the Prohibitionist Counterattack in Canada. Analysis by Richard Cowan
and
Canadian Medical Cannabis Patients Denounce Health Canada's War On Sick And Dying As New Survey Shows MARIJUANA LAWS A TOTAL FAILURE
and
 The Prohibitionist Counterattack in Canada Escalates. Blatant Drive to Create DEAland Style Police State. Phony Decrim Bill Gets Even Worse.
and
 D oh! Canada? Proposed Marijuana Modernization Equals The Sum of All Their Ignorance. The Intellectual and Moral Bankruptcy of Canadian Cannabis Prohibition. Analysis by Richard Cowan

The article by Chad Skelton echoed the prohibitionist complaint that Fewer than one in seven people convicted of growing marijuana in B.C. over the past two years was sentenced to any time in jail, according to court statistics provided to The Vancouver Sun.

And growers were even less likely to face jail time in Vancouver -- where fewer than one in 13 received a jail sentence.

In fact, 59% of BC growers and 83% of Vancouver growers received neither jail time nor a fine. They did received probation or a conditional sentence to be served at home. Inspector Paul Nadeau, head of the RCMP's Coordinated Marijuana Enforcement Team, is quoted as saying that he believes growers are increasingly moving to B.C. from other provinces and U.S. states where sentences are harsher.

However, the article does not cite a single case in which an American had been charged with growing, much less getting a lax sentence. But a nark said it, so it must be true. That is the fundamental premise of journalism in the age of prohibition.
See
 Dan Gardner of The Ottawa Citizen Continues Iconoclastic Practice of Questioning Government Statements And Checking Facts. Someday These Techniques May Even Be Taught In Journalism Schools.

In a triumph of hope over experience, I decide to submit an Op-ed to the Sun, which I noted that they could shorten and run as a letter to the editor. There was no response, so here we have one more for the archives on a good anti-prohibitionist paper running prohibitionist propaganda without checking the facts. I made a few changes for clarity and added a few links.)
From 2001, See
 Why Do The Best Newspapers In Canada Keep Falling for the DEA/RCMP Party Line?

To the Editor of the Vancouver Sun:
January 20, 2005

Prohibition doesn't work, no matter how extreme the punishments.
By Richard Cowan

Your two part series on the punishment of BC marijuana growers began with the headline: Lax sentences attract U.S. growers, says drug inspector. ". However, neither article cited a single example of a U.S. grower who had been arrested here. Moreover, it did not offer any comparative data on US or Canadian sentences, nor did it demonstrate that higher US sentences had resulted in reducing the supply of cannabis.

Although US sentences for growing cannabis can sometimes be very cruel, a comparison with Washington State is informative. According to the DEA, California, Washington, Florida, Alaska, and Rhode Island accounted for nearly 62 percent of all indoor-cultivated cannabis plants eradicated in 2000.

Nonetheless, according to the state's Statistical Summary Of Adult Felony Sentencing Fiscal Year 2004only nine percent of first time offenders convicted of manufacturing or delivery of marijuana got actual prison time. That fact makes the BC numbers seem considerably less lax.

I asked well-known Seattle defense attorney Jeffrey Steinborn to comment on the article.

He said, My experience is that in State court, most first offenders get relatively minor sentences.

It varies from county to county. In King County (Seattle), there is virtually no jail time. Across the mountains, some of the counties like to give you the maximum (6 months county jail under current laws, although firearms may enhance that considerably.)

Those in Federal court less than 10% of the grow cases almost always go to prison. Nonetheless, we have huge numbers of people growing despite the well-publicized severe federal penalties.
(MarijuanaNews note: Smuggling cannabis into DEAland is something else.)
See
 A Leading Marijuana Lawyer Explains How the System Really Works A Must-Read, Especially for Canadians.

It's an economic crime and no amount of coercion or fear is going to keep the hungry, the desperate, the greedy and the foolish from taking advantage of these extremely inviting economic opportunities. For those with no resume' it's the best thing going.

We do, however, take their homes, cars, and usually their chances of getting a good job as a part of the package.

I thought Canadians were smart enough to realize that prohibition doesn't work, no matter how extreme the punishments.

In regard to Steinborn's last point, most economists and criminologists will tell you that it is the perceived likelihood of getting caught, not the severity of the possible sentence, that is the main deterrent to breaking the law. Most people simply don't think that they will be caught, and the perceived rewards for growing are always being touted by the police. That is why even harsh US federal sentences do not prevent large scale cultivation of cannabis.

In fact, the 2003 report by the UN's International Narcotics Control Board says, According to estimates of the United States Government, more than 10,000 tons of cannabis herb are produced in that country; in addition, more than 5,000 tons of cannabis are smuggled into the country. (Less than two percent comes from Canada.)
See
 Fantasy and Reality in UN and US Reports on The Global Drug War. The Real Numbers Are There. DEAland is The World's Largest Producer, Importer, and Consumer of Cannabis.

In other words, despite its sometimes vicious prosecutions, or because of the high prices that result, the US is the world's largest producer of herbal cannabis, ten times bigger than Canada, although roughly the same per capita. Is that the success Canadian police want to emulate?
See
 Time Magazine Reports BC Bud 20% Less Potent Than Four Years Ago?? Incompetent Prohibitionist Propaganda and Even Worse Journalism. As Some Reporters Die to Find the Truth Others Live to Lie.

Then there is the fact that Canada follows the European model on sentencing rather than the US model. Consequently, the US has roughly six times as many prisoners per capita as does Canada.
See
 The Patriot Act Hits A New Low As The Prison/Probation/Parole Population Hits A New High.

Andif sentences for cannabis cultivation are to be increased, do Canadians really want people to be punished more severely for growing a plant than for crimes of violence?

For example, according to the 2003 StatsCan report Sentenced cases and outcomes in adult criminal court, the median sentence for Major assault was only 75 days. In fact, the median sentence for rape was only 360 days. For a serious property crime like burglary (breaking and entering) the median sentence was only 150 days.

If Canadians really want to increase the penalties for all crimes, are they prepared to bear the economic and social costs of greatly expanding its prison system?

It is ironic that Tuesday's Sun also reported that A federal medium-security prison in British Columbia has become a powder keg because of lax enforcement by its management Also, searches in December turned up a higher than usual amount of drugs and alcohol. Is this the prison to which marijuana growers are to be sent?

In your excellent editorial on the subject, Want stiffer sentences for grow-ops? Lobby MPs, not judges, you rightly point out that the Parliament has urged that the courts avoid sending offenders to prison whenever possible.

However, before British Columbians and other Canadians start urging the Parliament to increase sentences for growing cannabis, they should consider all the facts. As Jeff Steinborn said, Prohibition doesn't work, no matter how extreme the punishments.
